name: CryptanalysisBench
description: CryptanalysisBench is a benchmark of formal cryptanalytic security games for evaluating the ability of LLM-based agents to find and exploit weaknesses in real-world cryptographic algorithms. Each task wraps a reference C implementation of a cryptographic algorithm in a uniform CLI shim and exposes one or more security games (e.g., key recovery, indistinguishability, AEAD tag forgery, KEM private-key recovery, hash collision/preimage, signature forgery) via a FastAPI game controller. An agent must produce a self-contained attack script that wins the chosen game; a verifier grades the attack against an automated test harness. The benchmark covers 191 algorithms (49 T1, 135 T2, 7 Cbase), drawn primarily from four NIST standardization processes (AES, SHA-3, Lightweight Cryptography, Post-Quantum Cryptography), spanning efficiently-broken schemes (T1), schemes with only slow or no known attacks (T2), and frontier modern primitives exposed at full strength (Cbase) or in round-reduced challenge variants (C), across symmetric ciphers, AEAD, hash functions, KEMs, public-key encryption, and digital signatures. For T2 and Cbase algorithms, generate_harbor_tasks.sh additionally emits scaled-down difficulty variants (easy/medium/hard) from the patches under variant_patches/.

distribution.name: repository
distribution.description: Public git repository of CryptanalysisBench, containing algorithms/, security_game_framework/, generate_harbor_tasks.sh, and tasks_manifest.csv.

distribution.name: tasks_manifest.csv
distribution.description: One row per cryptanalysis task in the benchmark, with the security class, scheme type, upstream algorithm source URL, allowed security games, presence of a reference solution, and per-task agent/verifier timeouts.

distribution.name: algorithm-tasks
distribution.description: Per-algorithm task folders. Each folder contains task.toml (Harbor task metadata), environment/algorithm_src/ (upstream C reference implementation plus build_cli.sh, cli.c, cli_stdin.h), environment/possible_security_games.yml (allowlist of compatible security games), optionally solution/solve.sh (reference attack used by the oracle agent), and, for algorithms with scaled-down variants, generate_variants.sh plus variant_patches/ (parameter-reduction patches applied at build time).

distribution.name: security-game-framework
distribution.description: Shared framework merged into every task: FastAPI game controller, the security-game implementations under environment/game-controller/security_games/, the agent-facing CLI client, the agent instruction template, and the verifier test harness.

distribution.name: generate_harbor_tasks.sh
distribution.description: Build script that combines algorithms/<algo>/ with security_game_framework/ into a runnable Harbor task folder tasks_<DATE>/<algo>/.

recordSet.name: tasks
recordSet.description: One record per cryptanalysis task in the benchmark, sourced from tasks_manifest.csv.

field.name: task_name
field.description: Folder name under algorithms/, e.g. T1_rvb or Cbase_aes.

field.name: security_class
field.description: Difficulty/brokenness tier inferred from the folder prefix: T1 (efficiently breakable), T2 (only slow attacks or no attacks known), Cbase (frontier modern primitives at full strength), C (frontier round-reduced challenge variants).

field.name: scheme_type
field.description: Cryptographic scheme family inferred from the allowed security games: symmetric, aead, hash, kem, asymmetric_pke, signature.

field.name: algorithm_source_url
field.description: URL of the upstream reference implementation, copied verbatim from algorithms/<task>/task.toml [metadata].algorithm_source.

field.name: allowed_security_games
field.description: Semicolon-separated list of security-game class names this task is compatible with (subset of the framework's possible_security_games.yml).

field.name: has_solution
field.description: Whether algorithms/<task>/solution/solve.sh exists. The oracle agent uses these reference solutions to sanity-check that the task is solvable.

field.name: agent_timeout_sec
field.description: Wall-clock budget (seconds) the agent has to produce an attack script.

field.name: verifier_timeout_sec
field.description: Wall-clock budget (seconds) the verifier has to grade the attack across all attack rounds.

rai:dataLimitations: Coverage is curated, not exhaustive: the benchmark contains 191 algorithms, biased towards NIST submission packages (AES, SHA-3, Lightweight Cryptography, PQC) plus a handful of classical and modern ciphers. It is not representative of all deployed cryptography.
Each task targets a specific formal security game; a 'broken' result on one game does not transfer to other adversarial models or to the algorithm's overall security.

Tasks in the Cbase / C (frontier) tiers are expected to remain unbroken by current LLM agents and produce saturated 0-reward signals; they serve as upper-bound stressors rather than discriminative items.
The verifier grades attack-script success against an automated test harness with finite attack rounds, not a formal cryptographic proof of insecurity.

Scaled-down variants are approximate: the parameter reductions (partly proposed with LLM assistance) can introduce weaknesses unrelated to the original design (scaling artifacts), and a break of a variant does not imply a break of the full-strength primitive.
Reference implementations are kept as originally published, including their bugs; some tasks can be solved by exploiting an implementation defect rather than a weakness of the underlying design.
Most T1 attacks are old and publicly documented, so success on T1 may reflect recall of published cryptanalysis rather than independent rediscovery.
rai:dataBiases: Algorithm selection is biased towards NIST-submission candidates (AES, SHA-3, lightweight cryptography, PQC). Algorithms with publicly available reference implementations and accompanying cryptanalysis literature are over-represented relative to proprietary or unpublished schemes.

Within the T1 (efficiently breakable) tier, algorithms are over-represented relative to their real-world deployment, by design: the goal is to test agent capability against weaknesses that are recoverable in principle, so the tier intentionally collects schemes that have well-documented attacks.
Difficulty tiers (T1/T2/Cbase/C) are assigned by the authors based on published cryptanalysis at the time of curation; this judgement may drift as new attacks are discovered.
The benchmark surfaces only English-language documentation and attack literature; cryptanalysis published only in other languages is under-represented.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The benchmark contains no personal data, no human subjects, no demographic information, no medical data, and no proxy information about individuals. All artifacts are cryptographic algorithm source code (typically C reference implementations) plus task configuration files (TOML, YAML), a Python framework for the game controller, and shell build scripts.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation of LLM-based agents (claude-code, terminus-2, oracle, and other harnesses) on a precisely-specified suite of cryptanalytic security games.
Comparative scoring of agent capabilities across cryptographic scheme families (symmetric ciphers, AEAD, hash, KEM, public-key encryption, signatures) and across difficulty tiers.
Authoring and validating new security games or new task algorithms by extending the framework under security_game_framework/.
Stress-testing the security of cryptographic algorithms against LLM-based agents.
Out-of-scope use cases: training data for general-purpose code LLMs and production cryptographic guidance.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Positive impact: improves the rigour with which AI agents are measured on a scientifically grounded class of security tasks, lowers the bar to running such evaluations by packaging 191 reference implementations in a uniform CLI contract, and supports stress-testing of candidate schemes before standardization or deployment. Risk: the benchmark is dual-use and publishes reference attack scripts (solution/solve.sh) for 51 tasks: all 49 T1 algorithms and two T2 algorithms (RankSign and SpoC). Mitigations: (1) T1 is restricted to algorithms with publicly known practical attacks, and the RankSign script follows a published attack; (2) the SpoC script implements a key-recovery attack found by LLM agents during this work that was, to the authors' knowledge, previously unpublished; SpoC is a NIST Lightweight Cryptography candidate that was not selected for standardization; (3) no previously unpublished attacks on standardized or widely deployed cryptography are released; (4) the security games are formal academic models, not exfiltration tooling.
prov:wasDerivedFrom: Reference implementations of each cryptographic algorithm. Per-task upstream URLs are recorded in algorithms/<task>/task.toml under [metadata].algorithm_source and surfaced in tasks_manifest.csv (column algorithm_source_url). Sources include NIST PQC, SHA-3 and Lightweight Cryptography submission packages (csrc.nist.gov, csrc.nist.rip), archived AES-candidate and other historical sources (web.archive.org, schneier.com), the BIKE suite (bikesuite.org), Classic McEliece (classic.mceliece.org), NTRU Prime (ntruprime.cr.yp.to), and a small number of original-author repositories on GitHub. Full-strength tasks use each source unmodified except for a thin uniform CLI shim (cli.c + cli_stdin.h) added by the authors; scaled-down variants additionally apply the parameter patches under variant_patches/.
prov:wasGeneratedBy: Per-task CLI shim (cli.c + cli_stdin.h) authored by the benchmark authors to provide a uniform 'key: value' line-oriented interface on top of each upstream reference implementation's native API (e.g., crypto_aead_encrypt for AEAD, crypto_kem_keypair for KEMs).

Security-game framework (security_game_framework/) authored from scratch: FastAPI game controller, per-game stage logic under environment/game-controller/security_games/, the agent-facing client CLI, the agent instruction template, and the pytest-based verifier in tests/.

Build pipeline: generate_harbor_tasks.sh copy-merges algorithms/<algo>/ with security_game_framework/ (cp -rn semantics, so algorithm-specific files override framework defaults), runs prepare_prompt.py to substitute timeout placeholders, and emits a self-contained tasks_<DATE>/ folder runnable by Harbor.

Scaled-down variants: per-algorithm generate_variants.sh scripts apply the committed patches under variant_patches/ to reduce rounds, key sizes, or other parameters, producing easy/medium/hard variants. Where established conventions exist (e.g. round-reduced AES and ChaCha) standard reduced versions are used; for the remaining algorithms the parameter choices were proposed with the assistance of an LLM (Claude Opus 4.8) given the scheme specification, targeting roughly 2^30-2^40, 2^40-2^60 and 2^60-2^80 operations.

Synthetic plaintexts, keys, nonces, and other random values are produced at runtime by each algorithm's CLI from a CSPRNG (/dev/urandom). No human annotation, no crowdsourcing, no scraping of user-generated content.
